description: Day 2 Stream 1 talks from BSides Las Vegas 2021.

talks.title: A Fireside Chat
talks.teaser: Explores disinformation, software supply chain risk, and policy levers for better security, from a former federal cyber official's view.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with social media as both a tool and a hazard. Early WannaCry indicators surfaced on Twitter, yet the same platforms have spread propaganda and eroded trust. The speaker names five overlapping groups behind disinformation: foreign intelligence services, political activists, conspiracy communities, anti-vaccine groups and profiteers. Education is offered as a partial remedy, including a 2019 government awareness campaign that used a pineapple-pizza debate to explain how influence operations unfold.

The middle section covers software supply chains. The speaker argues the attacks are not new, but their reach is growing because adversaries target single points of leverage such as widely used vendors. Outsourcing shifts risk to third parties without removing it, and basic practices remain hard. He describes an executive order requiring software bills of materials and stronger build and testing requirements, while raising concerns about cost and small vendors. Product labeling, a shared vocabulary, and better protection for industrial control systems and rural utilities also come up.

The closing turns more optimistic. The speaker sees progress where executives treat security as a differentiator and empower security leaders to act. He encourages skepticism toward any single news source and reflects on leadership lessons about empathy. His final point is that risk is managed continuously rather than eliminated.

talks.title: Repo Jacking: How GitHub exposes over 70,000 projects to remote code injection
talks.teaser: Explains how reclaimed GitHub usernames let attackers hijack repositories and inject code into dependent open-source projects.
talks.summary:
The talk examines repo jacking, a supply chain weakness in which a GitHub username that has been renamed or deleted can be registered by anyone else. Any dependency that still points at the old name then loads code from the new owner's account, which can lead to code injection without the dependent project changing anything. The speaker describes how the issue was first noticed during a code review, when a dependency URL redirected to a different repository and, once the original account was free, could be taken over.

The speaker explains why renames and transfers are more dangerous than outright deletions, because GitHub's repository redirects keep old URLs working and so hide the exposure. GitHub's earlier mitigation blocked re-registration only for repositories with more than 100 clones in the week before a rename, which the speaker judged insufficient for small, rarely cloned libraries. The mass analysis combined GitHub's source archive with libraries.io dependency data, finding roughly 50,000 unregistered usernames, about 18,000 directly vulnerable projects, and around 70,000 impacted projects once transitive dependencies were followed to depth five.

For practitioners, the main advice is to avoid linking directly to GitHub repositories and to rely on package managers instead. Where direct links cannot be avoided, pinning to a full commit hash is safer than pinning to a tag or branch, though the speaker found that pinning can be bypassed in some package managers. Lock files help only where they carry integrity checks for the fetched code.

talks.title: Lessons Drawn From Cybersecurity In The Rise of Privacy Tech
talks.teaser: Panelists compare privacy and security practices across product, sales, communications and startup accountability.
talks.summary:
The panel opens by treating privacy and security as overlapping but distinct disciplines. The speakers argue that practitioners need clear definitions inside their own organizations, while speaking plainly to journalists, consumers and executives who often do not separate the two. Privacy tech, in their framing, is technology aimed at privacy problems, and compliance tools are only one part of it. They also argue for setting privacy requirements early, before systems are built, in the same way security has moved left.

Much of the discussion borrows from the security field. Developers, the panel says, want products that are fast, durable and widely used, so privacy can be presented as part of product quality rather than a blocker. Privacy is described as controlled sharing with respect for context, not just secrecy. On sales, the speakers suggest identifying the person who truly benefits from a product rather than relying on job titles, and helping legal and procurement teams buy software-as-a-service. In communications, they stress that internal practice must match external messaging, that privacy claims need evidence, and that communications staff should join product reviews before launch.

The closing message is that privacy tech vendors face a skeptical audience, so every claim should be backed by documented behavior. Startups are advised to be candid about where they stand and to bring communications and legal input in early.

talks.title: Virtualizing Your Ford SYNC3 for Fun and Profit
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a QEMU-based virtual Ford SYNC 3 setup for infotainment research without a real car.
talks.summary:
The researchers wanted to study Ford's SYNC 3 infotainment unit without risking a test vehicle or paying for costly development boards. They chose the version found in a Lincoln MKZ, a car widely used as a base for autonomous vehicle testing, and noted that its firmware update images were publicly downloadable. Existing hardware options were either too expensive or too limited for debugging and fuzzing, so they built a virtual machine for the QNX-based system on QEMU.

Getting the emulator to boot required patching the SD card driver, where a race between threads in the guest left the card undetected under emulation. Debugging was difficult because the QNX debugger does not support local sessions, so the team built a tunnel that carried TCP traffic over a virtual serial port. A later version added a custom register channel with signalling, which was much faster. The talk also covered unpacking the update archives, rebuilding images with extra libraries, and running the Bluetooth stack against a fake serial port and a simple virtual host controller.

The main finding was a command injection flaw in the update application, where crafted archive names reached a shell, and the team also reported two Bluetooth stack issues. Ford's later changes addressed the update problem, while the company treated attacks requiring physical access or a man-in-the-middle as out of scope. The practical takeaway is that a low-cost virtual setup can make embedded automotive research workable without owning the vehicle, though reverse engineering without a live car remains slow.

talks.title: Manage Your Attack Surface on a Budget
talks.teaser: Shows how a homegrown open-source tool maps exposed external assets and finds sensitive data internally on a tight budget.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the problem of knowing what you are defending. Organizations have data centers, headquarters and satellite sites, and a single misconfigured host can be found by attackers using internet scanners. The speakers cite Verizon breach report findings on misconfigurations and old internet-facing vulnerabilities as evidence that exposure is a common cause of incidents.

The middle covers Scout, a homegrown tool for external attack surface management. It works in stages: connect registrars and cloud accounts, enumerate IPs and DNS names, query internet search data sources, run port and banner checks, establish a baseline with the security operations team, then send alerts to chat or ticketing. The team said the largest hurdle was building the baseline, and moving scanning work to serverless cloud services cut scan time from about 28 days to roughly 12 hours. A second component, Scout Internal, looks for sensitive data copied to developer workstations and other sites, using regex-based PII detection, and it faced access, new database type and latency challenges.

The closing portion compares the homegrown approach with commercial products: it is customizable but needs senior engineers and integration work. Practical advice includes starting from accounting records to find services in use, running the scanner from a cloud instance, and treating IoT and SBOM aggregation as next steps. Privacy laws across regions shaped how scanning was scoped by country.

talks.title: All your Ether are belong to us (a.k.a Hacking Ethereum-based DApps)
talks.teaser: Walks through reentrancy, integer overflow and on-chain data exposure in Ethereum DApps, with a live demo of each bug.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short primer on blockchain: a distributed ledger protected by hashes and proof-of-work consensus, with smart contracts being code stored on-chain that anyone can read and call. It then explains how a hybrid decentralized app pairs static web files served from a normal server with a backend on Ethereum, and how a browser wallet signs transactions that are relayed through a node.

The middle section is the core of the session. A betting game that kept player choices as "private" data showed that every transaction is public, so the opponent could read the move and win. An overflow in a token sale let a purchase total wrap around to a tiny payment for a very large token balance. A reentrancy flaw in a simple deposit contract was exploited with a malicious fallback function that kept withdrawing funds in a loop until the victim contract was empty.

For fixes, the presenter recommends keeping sensitive data off-chain or encrypted, using safe math libraries or Solidity 0.8 and later, and updating balances before sending funds, plus adding a reentrancy lock. Static and dynamic tools help but cover limited ground, so manual review and reading the contract logic matter most. The Q&A covers bug bounties, which often pay in the project's own token, and upgradeable proxy patterns as a way to work around immutability.

talks.title: Securing the 2020 Presidential Campaign: Threats, Challenges, and a Global Pandemic!
talks.teaser: Panelists from 2020 US presidential campaigns describe securing staff, vendors and fundraising during the pandemic.
talks.summary:
This panel looks at how US presidential campaigns run and why their security is difficult. Panelists from the DNC, the Biden campaign, a campaign data firm and the fundraising platform ActBlue explain that a campaign behaves like a startup with a fixed end date: thousands of staff join and leave within months, and many vendors are one- or two-person shops. During the primaries, the DNC offered security guidance to more than twenty campaigns before a nominee was known, so that whoever won would start from a solid baseline.

The discussion then turns to 2020, when the pandemic pushed campaigns fully remote. Staff were onboarded without anyone touching their laptops, so teams leaned on a basic checklist covering updates, two-factor authentication, password managers and hardware security keys. Panelists described support sessions for people new to security keys, shortages of Chromebooks, and a discount program for federal campaigns that made keys cheaper. Software left over from earlier cycles was reviewed and shared as common infrastructure rather than rebuilt every four years. Disinformation and attacks on donation flows were also named as newer concerns.

For practitioners, the panel stressed that security must stay a priority between election cycles, since a lack of major incidents can make it look unnecessary. Controls should be secure by default and easy to use, and hiring for security and IT roles was encouraged ahead of the 2022 and 2024 cycles.

talks.title: JOINing Across the Stack: Structured Security Analytics for the modern attack surface
talks.teaser: Shows how SQL queries over osquery, cloudquery and kubequery can join endpoint, cloud and Kubernetes telemetry.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem that an organization's attack surface now spans laptops, servers, containers, cloud accounts, SaaS applications and identity providers. Each cloud provider exposes its own APIs and data formats, so visibility ends up split across many silos and defenders struggle to ask consistent questions.

The speaker presents structured security analytics as a set of open-source tools that turn this data into SQL tables. osquery covers hosts, endpoints and virtual machines, with scheduled and real-time queries and results that can be shipped to a file, a socket or a streaming pipeline. cloudquery extends the same approach to AWS, GCP and Azure resources, and kubequery covers Kubernetes clusters as a daemon set. A minimal upstream endpoint, query tls, can collect the results. The middle of the talk walks through a hypothetical intrusion in which stolen IAM credentials launch an instance, a script reads sensitive data from an S3 bucket and a curl command sends it out. Cloud API tables are paired with host process, socket, DNS and file tables, and the results can be checked against domain, IP and TLS fingerprint reputation data to follow each stage. Other examples include checking S3 encryption and versioning settings against CIS benchmark guidance and testing IAM password policy requirements, with a short live demo of the password policy check.

The main takeaway is that a team already fluent in SQL can apply the same query skills across endpoints and cloud platforms, and that scheduled queries build a history useful for drift monitoring and compliance. The speaker notes that the cloud tables are still being expanded and that some returned fields remain raw JSON, so coverage is partial.

talks.title: A Serverless SIEM: Detecting All Baddies
talks.teaser: Explains how a cloud-native, serverless SIEM on Google Cloud ingests logs, runs detections, and automates alert handling.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why a detection and response team chose to build its own SIEM instead of running an existing one. The speakers described the pain points of their earlier setup: patching a self-hosted cluster, slow or failing searches, weak scaling during large attacks, and the need for logging agents on every server. Their requirements covered global log intake, efficient and safe transfer, fast search, easy rule authoring, industry-standard rule formats, and low cost.

The architecture runs on Google Cloud with no servers to manage. Logs arrive through several paths: writes to storage buckets that trigger processing, native exports into BigQuery, and scheduled pulls from SaaS audit APIs every few minutes. Detections come in two styles: stream rules written in CEL that evaluate each event, and batch rules written as SQL on BigQuery schedules. Rules live in version control with Sigma-style formats and editor tooling. A notification component deduplicates repeated alerts into a single ticket and routes them to chat, Jira, or PagerDuty. An Airflow-based automation layer enriches alerts and can ask users to confirm suspicious activity.

The speakers put storage cost at roughly 50 to 70 cents per gigabyte with a year of searchable retention, and noted that about half of their spend came from an optional hot-search logging tier. Development, staging, and production environments are all managed with Terraform. Next steps include log normalization, threat intelligence integration, and more understandable anomaly detection. In the Q&A they warned about cloud billing traps, such as unpartitioned BigQuery tables, and said open-sourcing parts of the project is on the roadmap.

talks.title: Closing
talks.teaser: Recaps a virtual blue-versus-red training game, covering how defenders hunted persistence and how attackers kept access.
talks.summary:
This closing segment of the Pros vs. Joes game at BSidesLV 2021 gives an after-action look at a virtual blue-versus-red training exercise that ran for about 36 hours. The organizers explain that the game is meant to grow newer defenders by pairing them with professional attackers on a shared set of network assets. The red cell had early access to the environment and used persistence, default credentials, web shells and several command-and-control tools across Windows and Linux systems, while blue teams worked to find and remove those footholds.

The panelists described how defenders hunted for rogue accounts, unexpected SSH keys, respawning binaries and misconfigurations, using hardening benchmarks and attack-framework thinking to guide their work. They said removing persistence mattered more than patching, since red could often regain root through backdoored binaries without needing an exploit. A mid-event purple phase let blue players try offensive techniques, and paid consulting sessions let red members coach blue teams on specific systems. The game closed with a final scorched-earth hour in which both sides were free to disrupt the remaining hosts.

The main takeaway is that the exercise rewards learning on both sides. Participants said it built practical skills faster than routine work, and they encouraged people interested in security careers to spend time on both offense and defense.
